info.bio: Grupo fundado en 1980 por los también componentes de Talking Heads, Tina Weymouth y Chris Frantz. Sus mayores éxitos fueron "Wordy Rappinghood", "Genius of Love", "Under the Boardwalk", "Suboceana" y "Sunshine and Ecstacy".

scenes.name: Funk industrial
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Tras la caída de P-Funk, muchos ritmos nuevos vinieron de fuera: Kraftwerk, Art of Noise («Beat Box», «Close (to the Edit)»), Talking Heads (Stop Making Sense, con Bernie Worrell) y el «Genius of Love» de Tom Tom Club. Herbie Hancock pidió a su mánager Tony Meilandt unos temas de hip hop y con Bill Laswell y Grandmixer D.S.T. hizo «Rockit» (Future Shock, 1983): la cima del funk industrial nada más empezar. Laswell (Material, Time Zone con John Lydon, Manu Dibango, los Last Poets) dejó su sello de bajo grueso; sellos como Celluloid, On-U Sound, Tommy Boy o Def Jam sacaban ritmos ásperos de raspados metálicos y tensión de Guerra Fría. On-U Sound de Adrian Sherwood fichó a la sección rítmica de Sugarhill (Doug Wimbish, Skip McDonald, Keith LeBlanc): Tackhead, el «No Sell Out» con la voz de Malcolm X, «el P-Funk de los ochenta» según Pedro Bell.
scenes.family: Hip hop, go-go y funk de los noventa

scenes.name: Talking Heads
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Estudiantes de la Escuela de Diseño de Rhode Island que no querían ser llamados art rock: imagen «normal» y pulcra frente al cuero del CBGB, guitarra «finita, limpia y metálica» de David Byrne, el bajo melódico de Tina Weymouth con slap a lo Larry Graham y Jerry Harrison (ex Modern Lovers) a los teclados. Con «Psycho Killer» fundan los nervios de la new wave, pero siempre con funk, tocado como blancos de clase media. Brian Eno, casi un quinto miembro y su George Martin, produce una trilogía de «funk psicodélico» inspirada en Parliament-Funkadelic: More Songs About Buildings and Food («Take Me to the River»), Fear of Music (la desorientación de 1979, «Life During Wartime», «I Zimbra» con un poema de Hugo Ball) y Remain in Light (1980), afrofunk construido con improvisaciones recortadas en el estudio, polirritmo y predicadores radiofónicos: «una obra maestra». Las tensiones por la autoría con Eno llevan a un regreso al pop; Weymouth y Frantz triunfan con Tom Tom Club.
scenes.family: Art punk y new wave americana

mentions.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
mentions.author: Rickey Vincent
mentions.text: …of the strongest and loudest funk from a white band since the Average White Band back in 1974. A unique spinoff group from the Talking Heads, the Tom Tom Club, led by bassist Tina Weymouth, generated a club classic, “Genius of Love,” in 1982, one of the most sampled records of the eighties. Lyrics in the record praised funksters such as James Brown, Bohannon, and Bootsy Collins. One reason for the oozing funk flow of the Talking Heads and the Tom Tom Club was P-Funk keyboardist Bernie Worrell, who recorded with the group, performed with them on Soul Train, toured with the Talking Heads, and can be…

podcast.title: Formation as Side Project (1980)
podcast.body: Chris France and Tina Weymouth, while still members of Talking Heads, formed the Tom Tom Club in 1980. This new venture was characterized as a funky, dance-oriented band. "There were all those talking heads albums and then in 1980, they formed the Tom Tom Club, a funky dance-oriented band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Formation as Talking Heads Side Project (1981)
podcast.body: Tom Tom Club was formed in 1981 by Talking Heads' married rhythm section, Chris Frantz and Tina Weymouth, while David Byrne and Jerry Harrison were working on solo projects. The band was conceived at Compass Point Studios in the Bahamas. "Chris, France, and Tina Weymouth talking heads married rhythm section formed the band Tom Tom Club in 1981 while David Byrne and Jerry Harrison were working on solo projects."

podcast.title: Extensive Sampling of "Genius of Love"
podcast.body: "Genius of Love" became arguably the "most lucrative copyright" for any members of Talking Heads due to its frequent sampling. It has been sampled by numerous artists, including pop megastar Mariah Carey, British soul singer Mark Morrison, and rapper Latto (in 2022). "Genius of Love might also be the most lucrative copyright by any members of talking heads, as it has been sampled dozens of times..."

podcast.title: Funk Rock Hybrid Concept
podcast.body: Tom Tom Club was envisioned as a "funk rock hybrid" that aimed to celebrate "black American music and sounds from around the world," showcasing Frantz and Weymouth's diverse musical interests. "Tom Tom Club was intended as a funk rock hybrid that celebrated black American music and sounds from around the world."

podcast.title: Production Work for Other Acts
podcast.body: Chris France and Tina Weymouth also worked as producers for other musical acts, often in a collaborative "tag team" approach. Their production credits include the Happy Monday's "Yes Please" album in 1992, as well as contributions to records by Ziggy Marley, the Melvoin makers, and Gorillas. "They've also worked as producers for other acts and sort of a tag team way. And that includes the Happy Monday's and the Yes Please album in 1992."

podcast.body: Formed by Chris Frantz and Tina Weymouth, Tom Tom Club emerged as a creative outlet following their work with Talking Heads. "Chris and Tina are the Tom Tom Fub."

xref.title: Post-Breakup Projects
xref.body: Following their time with Talking Heads, the members pursued various projects: David Byrne embarked on a solo career, Jerry Harrison also engaged in solo work, and Chris Frantz and Tina Weymouth formed the group Tom Tom Club. "David Byrne has a solo career, Jerry Harrison does stuff on his own and Chris and Tina are the Tom Tom Fub."
